You could try running one of the other ones people posted. You can also try it in Firefox. Since Unkernel provides a Linux kernel and supports aarch64, one of the browsers should be able to run one of those, maybe one of the simpler ones. Here is the other comment in this thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50674542

another one they didn't mention: https://trynix.dev/

Since this thread is about Unkernel, you might be interested to know I got Doom running in it in realtime (with ascii graphics, but still):

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50602937

Not saying that a modern browser is simpler than Doom, but still, I think you might be able to get one of those to load. Someone successfully ran Postgres, which is very large and complicated.

Edit: nested, I was able to get as far as starting the smallest package I could find on trynix.dev, I just put in nano and then loaded the earliest version I could find. Here are the steps:

1. on your own computer open a tab in Chrome or Firefox and go to unkernel.dev and wait for it to load.

2. in the shell inside unkernel type:

    chromium
This downloads and starts it within the Linux environment your tab is running! It is very fast.

3. In the nested Chromium tab (inside unkernel.dev), go to trynix.dev and look for a very small package, for example nano and scroll down to an early version, select it and click boot.

It will then boot, so now you're running unkernel within unkernel. I got this working on a 2026 Mac mini. (24 GB of RAM).

For USB passthrough checkout https://github.com/gbl08ma/waarm64

It was posted recently and is similar in idea to unkernel but it goes further in virtualizing the hardware (and thus can run unmodified Linux kernels). Raw CPU performance is better but it uses more resources.

For a very rough comparison I like to think of it as unkernel is more like docker (kernel doesn't matter, you just want to run an app) while waarm64 is more like a real VM.

It's just so cool seeing the different approaches made possible using wasm and LLMs.

We are not in the era of humans finding / writing exploits for bugs, which this might have been a high bar for humans, but it is certainly not for swarms of frontier agents.

JS is bad enough to being abused by attackers against the (memory unsafe) browser engines running it. So I cringe from a security standpoint at this when everyone is believing that the next shiny object (WASM) is going to give some guarantee of isolation when it is untested against abliterated AI agents.
